q.q: What does ICT stand for?
q.why: ICT stands for Information and Communications Technology.

q.q: Where does your ICT teacher post lessons, handouts and homework?
q.why: Lessons, handouts and homework are uploaded to Google Classroom. MySchool is the website you log in to, not where the work is posted.

q.q: What is MySchool?
o: The app your teacher uses to mark homework and tests
A room in school where the computers are kept
The website you log in to with your school username and password
The name of the school's anti-virus software
q.why: MySchool is the website you log in to with your school username and password, and from it you can reach your school email and other tools.

q.q: You missed Tuesday's ICT lesson because you were ill. What should you do?
o: Leave out that week's homework, since you were not there when it was set
Catch up on the notes, homework and any test before the next lesson
Wait until your teacher sends you all the work you missed
Nothing, because it was not your fault you were absent
q.why: If you are absent it is your responsibility to catch up on homework, notes and any test before the next lesson.

q.q: In which year of KS3 ICT will you study website design?
q.why: Year 9 covers some new packages and applications plus website design.

q.q: In which year of KS3 ICT do you look 'under the hood' of a computer and start programming?
q.why: Year 10 covers what is under the hood of a computer plus an introduction to programming.

q.q: Why do pupils fill in the Pupil Baseline Survey at the start of Year 8?
o: To tell the teacher what computer equipment they can use at home
To choose which ICT class they would like to be put in
To set up their school email address and password
To test how much ICT they already know before lessons start
q.why: The survey is not a test; it tells the teacher what equipment you can use at home so problems can be spotted early.

q.q: You know you will miss next week's ICT lesson because of a school match. What is the best thing to do?
o: Tell your teacher beforehand so you might do the work early
Ask a friend to hand in your homework without telling the teacher
Wait until the end of term to catch up on everything
Say nothing and explain you were away when you get back
q.why: If you know you will be absent, tell your teacher beforehand; you may be able to do the work early.

q.q: Which excuse is NOT accepted for missing ICT homework?
o: I checked Google Classroom but the link was broken
I asked my teacher for help before the lesson
I was off sick and emailed my teacher
q.why: 'I wasn't here last lesson' is not accepted; you should ask a classmate, check Google Classroom or email your teacher.

q.q: What is an Acceptable Use Policy (AUP)?
o: A set of rules you agree to before you are allowed to use the computers
A program that blocks viruses on the school network
A list of websites that pupils are allowed to visit at home
A record of every file a pupil has saved on the network
q.why: An AUP is a set of rules you agree to before using the computers; it keeps you and the network safe.

q.q: What is the School Computer Contract?
o: An agreement that lets you install your own software
A bill for the cost of printing on school computers
A list of everyone's usernames and passwords
Your promise to follow the rules before using school computers
q.why: You sign the School Computer Contract to agree to follow the rules before you can use a school computer.

q.q: Why should you log off when you leave a workstation?
o: So your files are deleted for the next class
So the computer can install updates
So nobody else can use your account
To save electricity in the computer room
q.why: Leaving yourself logged in lets someone else act as you, and it would look like you did it.

q.q: Which of these is allowed on the school network?
o: Installing a game you brought from home
Logging in as a friend who forgot their password
Chatting to friends on a social network
q.why: The school network is for education, so researching homework is allowed.

q.q: Why is there a 'no food or drink' rule in the computer room?
o: It is only a rule during exams
It makes the keyboard keys harder to press
It smells and can damage the equipment
It slows down the school's internet connection
q.why: Food and drink smell and can damage equipment; the rule includes chewing gum.

q.q: What is a sanction?
o: A punishment for breaking the rules
A rule written in the Acceptable Use Policy
A record of the websites you have visited
A reward for using the computers well
q.why: Sanctions are punishments; using school computers for non-educational purposes brings sanctions.

q.q: What happens when a pupil tries to reach a blocked website in school?
o: Nothing, because blocked sites cannot be tried
The attempt is recorded on their account
The website opens after a short delay
q.why: Attempts to reach blocked sites are recorded on your account.

q.q: Sam logs in as his friend 'for a laugh' and posts a silly message. Why is this a problem?
o: It is fine because the friend did not mind
It breaks the rules and the message looks like it came from his friend
It only matters if the message contains a virus
It is fine as long as Sam logs off afterwards
q.why: Logging in as a friend breaks the rules, and anything done on that account looks like it was done by the friend.

q.q: Your teacher asks the class to turn their screens off. When should you do it?
o: Immediately, the first time you are asked
After you have saved and printed your work
When you have finished the task you are on
Only if the teacher asks you by name
q.why: Rule 3: turn your screen off immediately, the first time you are asked.

q.q: Which of the top 10 rules helps save resources such as paper and ink?
o: Save files often with sensible names
q.why: Only print when necessary: use print preview and sensible font sizes to save resources.

q.q: A pupil sends upsetting messages to a classmate using school email. What is this called?
q.why: Sending inappropriate or upsetting messages is cyberbullying, which is not allowed.

q.q: Which action breaks the Acceptable Use Policy?
o: Saving your work often with a sensible file name
Reporting a damaged keyboard to the teacher
Using print preview before printing a page
Copying text from a website and handing it in as your own work
q.why: The AUP says do not directly copy material from the internet and use it as your own work.

q.q: What is a computer?
o: A machine that stores and processes data by following instructions
A device that only connects people to the internet
A machine that can only ever do one job
A machine that thinks and has ideas of its own
q.why: A computer stores and processes data by following instructions in a program.

q.q: Why can the same computer be a word processor one minute and a game the next?
o: Because it has a different brain for each job
Because it decides for itself what to do
Because the internet tells it what to do
Because the program it follows can be changed
q.why: The program can be changed, so the same computer can do lots of different jobs.

q.q: Why can a computer not 'have ideas'?
o: It is not connected to the internet
It is too slow to think things through
It only follows the instructions in its program
It does not have enough storage space
q.why: A computer has no brain; it only does exactly what its instructions say.

q.q: What is the smallest number of computers needed to make a network?
q.why: A network is two or more computers joined together.

q.q: Which of these is NOT a network?
o: A single laptop that is not connected to anything
A gaming network such as Xbox network
Your home WiFi with a phone and a laptop
q.why: A single computer that doesn't share or send data with any other computer is not a network.

q.q: What is one benefit of joining computers into a network?
o: They no longer need any programs
Each computer can think for itself
They can share things like printers and files
q.why: A network lets computers communicate and share things like printers and files.

q.q: Who is in charge of the whole internet?
q.why: Nobody is in charge of the whole internet, so almost anybody can put almost anything on it.

q.q: Why can offensive or untrue material appear on the internet?
o: Nobody controls it, so almost anybody can put almost anything onto it
Viruses change true pages into untrue ones
Only experts are allowed to publish but some cheat
Google checks every page but sometimes makes mistakes
q.why: Because nobody is in charge of the whole internet, almost anybody can put almost anything onto it.

q.q: Why can the police often trace who posted something, even from a fake account?
o: Every post is signed with the user's real name
Every account has to show the owner's home address
Every device connected to the internet has an IP address
Social networks never allow fake accounts
q.why: Every device on the internet has an IP address, so you are not invisible online.

q.q: A pupil in Enniskillen plays an online game against someone in Australia. What makes this possible?
o: Both consoles are joined to the same home WiFi
Both players use the same User ID
Both consoles have the same games installed
Both consoles are connected to the internet
q.why: The internet is a worldwide network that lets computers all over the world communicate.

q.q: What is the main computer that controls the school network called?
q.why: All computers on the school network are controlled by a main computer called a server.

q.q: What is a workstation?
o: A printer shared by the whole class
The computer you sit at and use
The room where the server is kept
The main computer that controls the network
q.why: The computer you sit at and use is called a workstation.

q.q: Saving files 'centrally' on the school network means what?
o: They are copied to every pupil's area on the network
They are kept only on the workstation you saved them on
They are kept on a USB stick in the middle of the room
They are kept in one place so you can reach them from any computer in school
q.why: The server lets everyone save files centrally, in one place, so they can be reached from any school computer.

q.q: What is the name of the network used in schools throughout Northern Ireland?
q.why: The school network is part of C2k, which runs in schools across Northern Ireland.

q.q: What does your User ID tell the server?
o: That you are who you say you are
q.why: The User ID tells the server who you are; the password proves it.

q.q: What does a password do?
o: Proves you are who you say you are
Chooses which files you can print
q.why: Your password proves you are who you say you are.

q.q: Why must every User ID be unique?
o: So pupils can share an account
So it is easy for friends to guess
So the server knows exactly who is logged in
q.why: A unique ID identifies each person, so work can be traced and kept private.

q.q: Which password is the strongest?
q.why: It is long and mixes capitals, lower case, numbers and symbols.

q.q: What is the minimum length recommended for a strong password?
q.why: A strong password should have at least 8 characters.

q.q: Ella's username is ewilson22. Which would be the worst choice of password?
q.why: A password should never be the same as your username.

q.q: Why is 'Buster2012' a weak password even though it has a capital letter and numbers?
o: It is too long to remember
It is based on a name and has no symbols
q.why: A strong password should not be just a name and should include symbols as well.

q.q: Which is NOT a reason why everyone needs a unique login?
o: So nobody else can change your work
So that pupils can easily swap accounts
So your files are kept private
So actions can be traced to the right person
q.why: A unique login keeps files private and traceable; it is not meant for swapping accounts.

q.q: What is a folder?
o: A container that holds files and other folders
The part after the dot in a file name
A copy of a file kept in case the original is lost
One piece of saved work such as an essay
q.why: A folder is a container that holds files and other folders so they are organised.

q.q: Which of these is a folder, not a file?
q.why: Spreadsheets has no file extension, so it is a folder.

q.q: What is a file extension?
o: The name of the folder a file is saved in
The size of a file in megabytes
The date the file was last saved
The part after the dot that shows what type of file it is
q.why: The file extension is the part after the dot; it tells the computer the file type and which program opens it.

q.q: What type of file is 'holiday.png'?
q.why: .png (Portable Network Graphics) is an image file.

q.q: Which program makes .xlsx files?
q.why: .xlsx is an Excel spreadsheet.

q.q: What does .gif stand for?
q.why: GIF = Graphics Interchange Format.

q.q: Which file extension is used for a sound file?
q.why: .mp3 is a sound file; .mpeg and .avi are video and .tiff is an image.

q.q: Which of these file extensions is a video file?
q.why: .avi (Audio Video Interleave) is a video file, even though its name includes 'Audio'.

q.q: Which file extension belongs to Microsoft Access databases?
q.why: Access databases use .accdb; .xlsx is Excel, .pptx is PowerPoint and .docx is Word.

q.q: A file icon is an orange square with a P. Which extension will it most likely have?
q.why: The orange P icon is PowerPoint, which uses .pptx.

q.q: Alice's root folder is called Year 8 and inside it are subject folders. Where should she save a poem for English?
q.why: The poem belongs in the Poems topic folder inside the English subject folder.

q.q: In Alice's folder structure, what is 'Year 8'?
q.why: Year 8 is the root folder; subject folders sit inside it and topic folders inside those.

q.q: Which is the most meaningful file name for an email quiz in ICT?
q.why: Files should have meaningful names like Email Quiz.docx, not Document1.docx.

q.q: Which is a benefit of organising files into a folder structure?
o: You can save the same file in many places
Files no longer need file extensions
Files take up more storage space
It is easier to keep backups
q.why: Organised files are easier to find, easier to back up and do not waste storage on duplicates.

q.q: What does 'email' stand for?
q.why: Email is electronic mail, a message sent between computers over the internet.

q.q: Which of these is an example of email software rather than an email account or internet provider?
q.why: Outlook, webmail and Thunderbird are email software; BT and Plusnet are internet providers.

q.q: What is netiquette?
o: The list of people an email is sent to
A rule that emails must include an attachment
How you should behave when sending emails and using the internet
The software used to send email
q.why: Netiquette (net + etiquette) is how you should behave when sending emails and using the internet.

q.q: Why should you NOT type an email in capital letters?
o: It looks like you are shouting
It uses up more storage space
q.why: Typing in ALL CAPITALS looks like shouting.

q.q: Which is the best subject line for an email to your teacher about homework?
q.why: A good subject tells the recipient exactly what the email is about.

q.q: When is it acceptable to use an emoticon such as :) in an email?
o: In an email to a boss
In an informal email to a friend
In a formal email to a teacher
In the subject line of every email
q.why: Emoticons are fine in informal emails to friends but not in formal emails to a teacher or boss.

q.q: What is the recipient of an email?
o: The software used to send it
The subject line of the message
q.why: The recipient receives the email; the sender sends it.

q.q: After you send an email, where is a copy kept for you?
q.why: A copy is kept in the sender's Sent folder; the message appears in the recipient's inbox.

q.q: If your login username is jsmith456, what is your school email address?
q.why: Your school email address is your login username followed by @c2ken.net.

q.q: In your Outlook inbox, how can you spot an email you have not read yet?
o: It is shown in red text
It has a blue bar beside it
q.why: New (unread) emails have a blue bar; a paperclip shows an attachment.

q.q: Which message follows good netiquette when emailing a friend?
q.why: You should avoid ALL CAPS and text language, even with friends; a smiley is fine in an informal email.

q.q: What is the correct order to start a new email in school?
q.why: Log in to MySchool, click Office 365, select Outlook, then New Message.

q.q: What does CC stand for?
q.why: CC is carbon copy; BCC is blind carbon copy.

q.q: What is the difference between CC and BCC?
o: CC recipients can be seen by others; BCC recipients are hidden
CC sends the attachment; BCC sends only the text
CC recipients must reply; BCC recipients cannot reply
CC recipients are hidden; BCC recipients can be seen by others
q.why: Both get a copy, but BCC recipients are hidden from the other recipients.

q.q: A club secretary emails 200 members and doesn't want them to see each other's addresses. Which box should she use?
q.why: BCC hides recipients from each other.

q.q: You email Mr Butler and want your form teacher to see it for information. Where should your form teacher's address go?
q.why: CC sends a visible 'for your information' copy, like copying your form teacher into an email to Mr Butler.

q.q: Jack receives an email from Alex and sends it on to Robert. What has Jack done?
q.why: Sending an email on to someone new is forwarding.

q.q: What appears in front of the subject when you reply to an email?
q.why: RE: shows it is a reply; FW: shows it has been forwarded.

q.q: Robert receives an email with the subject 'FW: Match on Saturday'. What does this tell him?
o: Robert has been sent a hidden copy
The email has a file attached
Someone has passed on an email that was first sent to them
The sender is replying to an email Robert sent
q.why: FW: (or Fwd:) shows the email has been forwarded on.

q.q: When you click Reply, where does your message go?
o: To everyone in your contacts list
To your own Sent folder only
Back to the person who sent the email to you
To a new person whose address you type in
q.why: Reply sends a message back to the sender and fills in their address automatically.

q.q: What does a paperclip icon next to an email mean?
q.why: The paperclip shows the email has an attachment.

q.q: What is an attachment?
o: The first line of an email's message
A hidden copy of an email
The address of the person receiving an email
A file sent with an email
q.why: An attachment is a file, such as a Word document or photo, sent with an email.

q.q: Why should you sign off an email with your name?
o: So the recipient knows who it is from
So it is sent to the right address
So the subject line is filled in
So the email can be forwarded
q.why: Signing off with your name lets the recipient know who the email is from.

q.q: Which statement is correct?
o: The WWW is a collection of websites stored on the internet
The internet and the WWW are the same thing
The internet is a type of web browser
Email is part of the World Wide Web
q.why: The WWW is the websites; the internet is the network they are stored on.

q.q: Which of these is a web browser?
q.why: Chrome is a browser; Bing is a search engine.

q.q: Is the internet hardware or software?
o: Software: the web browser on your computer
Hardware: only the computers in your home
q.why: The internet is physical hardware such as cables, routers and servers; the WWW is the software/information.

q.q: In the 'roads and shops' comparison, what are the shops?
q.why: The internet is the roads and the WWW is the shops; email and gaming use the roads but are not shops on the web.

q.q: Which of these uses the internet but is NOT part of the World Wide Web?
q.why: Email and online gaming use the internet but are not part of the WWW.

q.q: What is a search engine?
o: A database that stores your saved files
A program such as Chrome that displays web pages
A tool such as Google or Bing that helps you find pages on the WWW
The cables and routers that make up the internet
q.why: Search engines like Google and Bing help you find pages on the WWW.

q.q: What is an algorithm?
q.why: Search engines use algorithms, which are sets of step-by-step rules.

q.q: In which search engine task is a website analysed and stored in a huge database?
q.why: Indexing analyses each website and stores it in the index.

q.q: What is a web crawler used for?
o: Showing the most relevant pages first
Storing web pages in a database
Displaying web pages on your screen
q.why: Crawlers (spiders) follow links to discover websites.

q.q: What is the correct order of the three search engine tasks?
q.why: Crawlers discover sites, they are indexed, then results are retrieved when you search.

q.q: Why should you check the top search result on more than one trustworthy site?
o: The top result is always an advert
The top result is always the least relevant
Anyone can publish on the web, so the top result is not always true
Search engines only show old pages first
q.why: The top result is not always true because anyone can publish on the web.

q.q: What is a computer virus?
o: A program designed to deliberately damage a computer or make it unreliable
A web page that shows untrue information
A program that scans files and removes harmful code
A fault in the hardware caused by dust or spilled drinks
q.why: A virus is a program designed to deliberately damage a computer system or make it unreliable.

q.q: Which of these is something a virus can do?
o: Update your other software for you
q.why: Viruses can corrupt or delete files, steal personal information and slow a computer down.

q.q: A virus has 'corrupted' Niamh's files. What does that mean?
o: The files have been copied to a USB stick
The files are scrambled so they won't open
The files have been sent to her teacher
The files have been moved to another folder
q.why: Corrupting files means scrambling them so they won't open.

q.q: Why must anti-virus software be kept up to date?
o: So it can recognise new viruses
So it makes the internet faster
So it can open email attachments for you
q.why: New viruses appear every day; old anti-virus software won't recognise them.

q.q: A friend gives you a USB stick with photos from the school trip. What should you do first?
o: Copy the photos to the school server
Email the photos to everyone in the class
q.why: A stick that has been in an infected computer can carry a virus, so scan it first.

q.q: Which email attachment is the most suspicious?
o: free_game.exe from someone you don't know
q.why: An unknown program from a stranger is high risk; attachments are a common way viruses spread.

q.q: What does anti-virus software do when it finds a virus?
o: Saves it in your Documents folder
Turns it into a safe file extension
Sends it on to your contacts
q.why: Anti-virus software removes or quarantines (locks away) anything it finds.

q.q: Which is the safest way to get a new game for your home computer?
o: Copy it from a USB stick without scanning it
Open a link a stranger emailed to you
Download it from a known, safe site with a parent's permission
Download a free copy from any site that offers one
q.why: Only download from known, safe sites, with permission from a parent or guardian.

q.q: Why are you not allowed to plug unknown devices into the school network?
o: They use up all of your file storage
They make the school printers stop working
They could carry a virus onto the network
q.why: Unknown devices could bring viruses, which is why you must not install software or plug them in on the school network.
